title: Stoichiometry and Reactions - Chemistry - Limiting Reagents
subject: Chemistry

questions.q: What defines the 'Limiting Reagent' in a chemical reaction?
options: The reactant that has the smallest mass
The reactant that is consumed completely first
The product formed in the largest amount
The reactant with the smallest coefficient
questions.explain: The limiting reagent is the reactant that runs out first, thereby limiting the amount of product that can be formed.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Consider the reaction: $2\text{A} + \text{B} \rightarrow \text{C}$. If you have 4 moles of A and 3 moles of B, which is the limiting reagent?
questions.explain: Ratio needed is 2 A : 1 B. With 3 moles of B, we need $3 \times 2 = 6$ moles of A. We only have 4 moles of A. Thus, A runs out first.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: In the reaction $N_2 + 3H_2 \rightarrow 2NH_3$, if 2 moles of $N_2$ react with 6 moles of $H_2$, what is the limiting reagent?
questions.explain: The ratio is 1:3. 2 moles of N$_2$ require $2 \times 3 = 6$ moles of H$_2$. Since we have exactly 6 moles, both are consumed completely.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Reaction: $2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. You have 4.0 g of H$_2$ and 40.0 g of O$_2$. Which is the limiting reactant? (H=1, O=16)
questions.explain: Moles H$_2$ = 4.0/2.02 = 1.98 mol. Moles O$_2$ = 40.0/32.00 = 1.25 mol. Reaction requires 2 mol H$_2$ for every 1 mol O$_2$. For 1.25 mol O$_2$, we need 2.5 mol H$_2$. We only have 1.98 mol H$_2$. Thus H$_2$ is limiting.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: In a reaction where Reactant A is the limiting reagent, what determines the theoretical yield?
options: The initial mass of Reactant B
The total mass of all reactants
The amount of product calculated from Reactant A
The experimental yield measured in the lab
questions.explain: Theoretical yield is calculated based on the complete consumption of the limiting reagent.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: For $S + 3F_2 \rightarrow SF_6$, if 4 moles of S are mixed with 10 moles of F$_2$, how many moles of SF$_6$ can be formed?
questions.explain: 4 mol S needs 12 mol F$_2$; we have 10 (Limiting). 10 mol F$_2$ produces $10 \times (1/3) = 3.33$ mol SF$_6$.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Given $4\text{Al} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$. If 4.0 moles of Al and 4.0 moles of O$_2$ react, how many moles of Al$_2$O​$_3$ are produced?
questions.explain: 4 Al needs 3 O$_2$. We have 4 O$_2$ (Excess). Al is limiting. 4 Al produces 2 Al$_2$O​$_3$.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Refer to the previous question ($4\text{Al} + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$). How many moles of the excess reagent (O$_2$) remain?
questions.explain: We used 3.0 moles of O$_2$ to react with 4.0 moles of Al. Started with 4.0 moles O$_2$. Remaining: $4.0 - 3.0 = 1.0$ mol.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: If 10.0 g of Calcium (Ca) reacts with 10.0 g of Oxygen (O$_2$) to form CaO ($2\text{Ca} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CaO}$), which reactant is in excess?
questions.explain: Moles Ca = 10/40.08 = 0.25 mol. Moles O$_2$ = 10/32.00 = 0.31 mol. Stoichiometry: 2 Ca : 1 O$_2$. 0.25 mol Ca needs 0.125 mol O$_2$. We have 0.31 mol O$_2$, so O$_2$ is in excess.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: What is the maximum mass of water produced from the reaction of 4.0 g H$_2$ and 32.0 g O$_2$?
questions.explain: $2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. 4g H$_2$ = 2 mol. 32g O$_2$ = 1 mol. Ratio is 2:1. Both are consumed exactly. Produces 2 mol H$_2$O. Mass = $2 \times 18.02 = 36.04 \text{ g}$.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Identify the limiting reagent when 3.0 moles of SO$_2$ react with 2.0 moles of O$_2$ to form SO$_3$ ($2\text{SO}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{SO}_3$).
questions.explain: Ratio 2 SO$_2$ : 1 O$_2$. 3.0 moles SO$_2$ require 1.5 moles O$_2$. We have 2.0 moles O$_2$ (Excess). So SO$_2$ is limiting.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Calculate the mass of CO$_2$ produced when 16.0 g of CH$_4$ reacts with 48.0 g of O$_2$ ($CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O$).
questions.explain: Moles CH$_4$ = 16/16 = 1. Moles O$_2$ = 48/32 = 1.5. CH$_4$ needs 2 moles O$_2$ (we only have 1.5). O$_2$ is limiting. 1.5 mol O$_2$ produces $1.5/2 = 0.75$ mol CO$_2$. Mass = $0.75 \times 44.0 = 33.0 \text{ g}$.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: In the synthesis of Ammonia ($N_2 + 3H_2 \rightarrow 2NH_3$), starting with 5 mol N$_2$ and 9 mol H$_2$, how many moles of NH$_3$ are formed?
questions.explain: 5 mol N$_2$ needs 15 mol H$_2$. We have 9 (Limiting). 3 mol H$_2$ -> 2 mol NH$_3$. 9 mol H$_2$ -> 6 mol NH$_3$.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Which statement best describes the reagent in excess?
options: It is completely consumed in the reaction
Some amount of it remains after the reaction stops
It has the largest molar mass
questions.explain: The excess reagent is the reactant that is not completely used up when the reaction is finished.
